opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
There is something uncomfortable but very true in today’s readings: the more successful we become, the easier it is to believe that we are in control.

In Ezekiel 28:1–10, the ruler of Tyre had become wealthy through his wisdom and business ability. He was intelligent, successful, and powerful. But somewhere along the way, those gifts became reasons for pride. He began to see himself as greater than he really was, almost as though he were God. God reminds him very plainly: you are a man, not God.

I think we can fall into this more easily than we realize. We work hard, build careers and businesses, accumulate possessions, gain experience, and learn how to solve problems. Eventually, we can begin to believe that because we have figured out many things, we can somehow control everything. But we cannot. Life has a way of reminding us how quickly circumstances can change. Money can disappear, careers can end, plans can fail, and the things we thought were secure may suddenly not be secure at all.

Then Jesus takes this further in Matthew 19:23–30 when He says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the Kingdom of God. The disciples are astonished and ask, “Who then can be saved?” I love that question because there is humility in it. They recognize something we all eventually have to recognize: we are only human. We have weaknesses, attachments, pride, and faults. How can any of us possibly make it?

Jesus answers, “For men this is impossible, but for God all things are possible.” Maybe that is where the hope is.

Jesus is not simply asking us to become poor or abandon everything good in our lives. He is asking whether there is anything we value more than following Him. Money, possessions, careers, family, plans, intelligence, accomplishments, and even our own ideas about how life should unfold can become things we hold onto too tightly. Following Christ sometimes means being willing to surrender what we thought our life was supposed to be.

And none of us does this perfectly. Salvation is not something we accomplish through our own intelligence, strength, success, or goodness. What we cannot accomplish ourselves, God can accomplish within us.

We all get a chance—a chance to recognize our pride, loosen our grip, stop believing that we control everything, choose differently, and follow Him again.

Perhaps the question for today is simply this: What am I holding onto so tightly that I would struggle to surrender it if God asked me to? Because eventually we discover that very little in this life was ever truly ours to control. But God was always there to trust.
